The AI Product Management internship in short

In the SkillMe AI Product Management internship you build SmartRecap: AI Meeting Notes Feature, a project where you take an AI feature from a rough idea to a PRD, an eval spec, a competitive analysis and a clickable prototype — the full product thinking loop, no repo required. In week 1 you pick a real AI feature idea (an AI meeting-notes summarizer for a team collaboration tool), talk to potential users about the problem, and study how existing products solve it. By week 4 you close the loop from idea to launch: write a lightweight launch plan and a metrics dashboard spec for measuring the feature post-launch, then publish a full case study telling the whole story from research to spec. Each milestone is posted on LinkedIn and checked against that week's checklist before it counts. Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month.

Week by week

What each week of the AI Product Management internship covers

The four milestones of SmartRecap: AI Meeting Notes Feature.

  1. Week 1 of 4

    Problem Framing and Competitive Analysis

    Beginner2-3 hours

    Pick a real AI feature idea (an AI meeting-notes summarizer for a team collaboration tool), talk to potential users about the problem, and study how existing products solve it. Good PM work starts with a sharp problem statement, not a feature list.

    What you learn

    • Framing an AI feature around a user problem, not a technology
    • Running short user interviews to validate a problem exists
    • Structuring a competitive analysis for AI features specifically
    • Writing a clear problem statement and success metric

    What you submit

    • Interview questions and notes, or survey results
    • A competitive analysis of 3 existing AI meeting-notes products
    • A one-paragraph problem statement
    • A defined success metric with a one-sentence justification
    How week 1 is reviewed
    • At least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are documented with direct quotes or notes
    • The competitive analysis names a specific gap or complaint for each of the 3 products, not just a feature list
    • The problem statement is grounded in a specific theme from your research, not a generic assumption
    • The success metric is measurable (you could describe exactly how you'd calculate it from real usage data)

    Stretch goal: Add a fourth competitor that is not an AI-first tool (e.g. plain manual meeting notes in Notion) to sharpen the specific value of the AI angle.

  2. Week 2 of 4

    PRD and Prompt/Eval Spec

    Beginner+2-3 hours

    Turn last week's research into a full PRD for the AI meeting-notes feature, plus a lightweight prompt and eval spec — the artifact that tells engineers not just what to build, but how to judge whether the AI part is actually working. This is the core skill that separates AI PM work from general PM work.

    What you learn

    • Structuring a PRD for a feature with a probabilistic (AI-generated) component
    • Writing user stories and acceptance criteria for an AI feature
    • Designing a lightweight prompt spec: inputs, instructions, and output format
    • Defining an eval spec: what 'good enough' output looks like and how to check for it

    What you submit

    • A full PRD covering problem, goals/non-goals, user stories and functional requirements
    • 4-6 user stories with objectively checkable acceptance criteria
    • A prompt spec defining inputs, instructions and required output format
    • An eval spec with 8-10 example cases and expected content plus a named failure mode
    How week 2 is reviewed
    • The PRD clearly separates goals from non-goals for this version
    • Every user story has acceptance criteria specific enough that two different readers would judge a real output the same way
    • The prompt spec is precise enough that someone else could write the actual prompt from it without asking clarifying questions
    • The eval spec names a concrete failure mode (like hallucination) and how you'd detect it, not just 'check if it's good'

    Stretch goal: Add a 'confidence' field to the required output format and write a rule for when the product should show a low-confidence warning to the user.

  3. Week 3 of 4

    Clickable Spec and Stakeholder Narrative

    Intermediate2-3 hours

    Turn the PRD into something people can actually react to: a clickable spec or lightweight prototype showing the feature in context, plus a stakeholder narrative explaining trade-offs. PMs ship decisions and clarity, not just documents — this week is about making the feature tangible before any engineer writes code.

    What you learn

    • Building a clickable spec or lightweight prototype without code (Figma, or a slide-based clickthrough)
    • Writing a stakeholder narrative that explains trade-offs, not just features
    • Anticipating and addressing likely engineering and design pushback in writing
    • Prioritizing scope for a first version (v1) versus later iterations

    What you submit

    • A clickable prototype or spec with at least 4-6 linked screens
    • A one-page stakeholder narrative covering rationale, scope and biggest risk
    • A list of 3 likely objections with planned mitigations
    • A v1 scope cut of the PRD's requirements with reasons for each cut
    How week 3 is reviewed
    • Someone unfamiliar with the project can click through the prototype and describe back what the feature does
    • The stakeholder narrative names a real technical risk, not a vague one, and ties it to your eval spec's failure mode
    • Each of the 3 objections has a specific, actionable mitigation, not just 'we'll be careful'
    • The v1 scope cut has a stated reason for every single item marked 'later'

    Stretch goal: Record a 60-second video walkthrough of the clickable prototype as if presenting it in a real stakeholder review meeting.

  4. Week 4 of 4

    Launch Plan, Metrics Dashboard Spec and Case Study

    Intermediate+2-3 hours

    Close the loop from idea to launch: write a lightweight launch plan and a metrics dashboard spec for measuring the feature post-launch, then publish a full case study telling the whole story from research to spec. This is the deliverable a hiring manager or team would actually read to judge your PM thinking end to end.

    What you learn

    • Writing a lightweight launch plan (phasing, rollout, guardrails)
    • Specifying a metrics dashboard for an AI feature (adoption, quality, safety signals)
    • Structuring a PM case study that tells a complete, honest story
    • Presenting a body of product work clearly to an outside reader

    What you submit

    • A lightweight launch plan with rollout phasing and a guardrail
    • A metrics dashboard spec with 6-8 metrics and their exact data sources
    • A stated kill-or-iterate decision rule tied to real metrics
    • A published end-to-end case study linking all four weeks of work, with a self-critical reflection
    How week 4 is reviewed
    • The launch plan names a specific, checkable condition for pausing or slowing rollout
    • Every metric in the dashboard spec has a named, plausible data source, not just a label
    • The kill-or-iterate rule references an actual number or threshold, not a vague 'if it's bad'
    • An outside reader can read the case study cold and accurately summarize the problem, the solution, and the biggest risk back to you

    Stretch goal: Write a one-paragraph 'v2' pitch for a natural next feature (e.g. auto-syncing action items to a task tracker) building on adoption data you'd expect from v1.

Is it for you?

  • You know the basics of PRDs, AI Evals and Roadmapping and want a real project to show for it, not more tutorials.

AI Product Management internship: questions and answers

Is this product management internship remote?

Yes. It is fully remote and open to students in any country, at about 2–3 hours a week.

Is it a general product management internship or only AI?

The project is an AI feature (SmartRecap, AI meeting notes), so you also write an eval spec. The rest, from problem framing and PRDs to metrics and launch plans, is core product management work.

What will I build in the AI Product Management internship?

You build SmartRecap: AI Meeting Notes Feature. Take an AI feature from a rough idea to a PRD, an eval spec, a competitive analysis and a clickable prototype — the full product thinking loop, no repo required. It is one project built up over four weekly milestones, so each week adds to the last.

What skills will I learn in the AI Product Management internship?

The AI Product Management internship works with PRDs, AI Evals and Roadmapping. Week 1: framing an AI feature around a user problem, not a technology; running short user interviews to validate a problem exists. Week 2: structuring a PRD for a feature with a probabilistic (AI-generated) component; writing user stories and acceptance criteria for an AI feature. Week 3: building a clickable spec or lightweight prototype without code (Figma, or a slide-based clickthrough); writing a stakeholder narrative that explains trade-offs, not just features. Week 4: writing a lightweight launch plan (phasing, rollout, guardrails); specifying a metrics dashboard for an AI feature (adoption, quality, safety signals).

Do I need experience to apply for the AI Product Management internship?

You need the basics of PRDs, AI Evals and Roadmapping, not prior internship experience. Week 1 starts at beginner level, where you pick a real AI feature idea (an AI meeting-notes summarizer for a team collaboration tool), talk to potential users about the problem, and study how existing products solve it. Week 4 reaches intermediate+ level. A short screening quiz (8 questions, about 5 minutes) checks you are ready to start.

How is each AI Product Management milestone reviewed?

Every week has a checklist, and a milestone is approved only when it meets all of it. For week 1 of SmartRecap: AI Meeting Notes Feature, that means: at least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are documented with direct quotes or notes; the competitive analysis names a specific gap or complaint for each of the 3 products, not just a feature list; the problem statement is grounded in a specific theme from your research, not a generic assumption; the success metric is measurable (you could describe exactly how you'd calculate it from real usage data). Reviewers include engineers who work at Walmart, Google and LinkedIn, and work that misses the bar comes back with notes.

What can I put on my resume after the AI Product Management internship?

Each approved milestone gives you a line you can back up with a public LinkedIn post: Interviewed real meeting attendees to validate a problem behind an AI feature idea; Ran a competitive analysis of 3 existing AI meeting-notes products and found real gaps; Wrote a grounded problem statement and a measurable success metric for an AI feature; Wrote a full PRD for an AI feature covering goals, non-goals and acceptance criteria; Designed a prompt and eval spec defining exactly what 'good' AI output looks like; Named a concrete AI failure mode (hallucination) and specified how to detect it; Built a clickable prototype to make an AI feature tangible before any code was written; Wrote a stakeholder narrative addressing real technical risk and scope trade-offs; Practiced cutting a v1 scope with clear, defensible reasoning for every deferred item; Wrote a launch plan and metrics dashboard spec with real data sources and a kill-or-iterate rule; Published a full PM case study taking an AI feature from research to launch plan; Got outside feedback on my case study and revised it for clarity before publishing.

Is the AI Product Management internship paid? Is there a stipend?

Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month. It is performance-based: 8–10 interns are picked each month from those who complete the internship and hold an issued certificate. It is not paid to every intern.

How much time does it take?

4 weeks, one milestone a week, each planned for about 2-3 hours. It is fully remote and open worldwide, so you work around college or a job.
